title: Hacker Runs Hermes AI Agent Unattended for Post-Exploitation at Thai Finance Ministry

reading.body:
An attacker deployed an autonomous AI agent called Hermes to conduct post-exploitation operations against Thailand's Ministry of Finance, operating the system without human oversight. The agent was run in YOLO mode, a configuration that bypassed safety prompts designed to prevent dangerous commands. This represents a model deployed in an adversarial context where the operator deliberately disabled the safety mechanisms that might have alerted defenders or prevented certain actions.

The deployment succeeded in part because the system operated unattended, allowing the attacker to maintain persistent access across multiple ministry systems and networks. The agent was used to automate the execution of privilege escalation exploits, creation of webshells, and credential theft. A human operator reviewing each command in real time, or alerts triggered by the disabled safety mode reaching defenders, could have interrupted this activity earlier.

It is not established whether the attacker's objective was espionage, whether all targeted systems were successfully compromised, or what data was ultimately exfiltrated beyond what appeared in the exposed directories.

summary:
# Summary

Thailand's Ministry of Finance was targeted by attackers using an autonomous AI agent called Hermes that operated without human oversight. Between July 9 and 13, 2026, researchers discovered three exposed directories on a Hong Kong server containing 585 files with exploit code, stolen credentials, and webshells. The attacker deployed a custom implant called Hades across Windows and Linux systems and used specially designed scripts to target the ministry's Hadoop infrastructure, GlassFish servers, and email systems. Security researchers notified Thailand's national cybersecurity authorities on July 15, 2026.

The Hermes agent logs showed the operator running the AI in YOLO mode, which bypassed safety prompts for dangerous commands. Investigators found evidence the attacker accessed multiple ministry systems, including administrative panels and internal networks. The operator used privilege escalation exploits targeting known vulnerabilities in Linux and Windows systems. While researchers could not confirm all systems were successfully compromised, the discovered materials and active session cookies indicate the attacker achieved authenticated access to several ministry networks.
